## Overview

This Adyen guide introduces tokenization for recurring payments. The 2026-09-15 snapshot calls Tokenize an Adyen Uplift module. With shopper consent, Adyen stores payment details in the Adyen Vault and the merchant later pays with a token representing those details. The page presents tokenization as a way to reduce exposure to sensitive payment data and PCI DSS scope; it does not establish current product packaging, merchant eligibility, enablement, or successful payment execution.

## Key takeaways

- Adyen documents two server-side implementation routes. Sessions creates a secure session for client-side components and is described as qualifying for SAQ A; Advanced gives the merchant more checkout control but requires the merchant to manage data flow and state.
- The documented recurring types are shopper-present one-click payments, regular merchant-initiated subscriptions, and automatic top-ups or other non-fixed schedule contracts. With Sessions, shopper-not-present token payments such as subscriptions still require a separate `/payments` call.
- Every stored token must be associated with a shopper reference that is unique to that shopper. Shopper references and tokens are merchant-account-scoped by default; sharing them across merchant accounts requires the separately enabled Token Groups feature.
- The guide says collecting raw card data requires full PCI DSS compliance. Using tokens can reduce PCI scope, but the snapshot is not a substitute for a merchant's current compliance assessment.
- The page routes readers to payment-method-specific recurring support and to separate guides for network tokens, Account Updater, forwarding stored details, creating tokens, and making token payments. Those linked pages were not read for this entry and provide navigation rather than evidence for their detailed behavior.

## Material qualifications

- Shopper consent is a condition for saving payment details.
- Creating a token and making a later payment are distinct actions; Sessions alone is not documented as executing shopper-not-present subscription or unscheduled payments.
- Token Groups is not the default scope and requires Support to enable it.
- This is a 2026-09-15 documentation snapshot. Product packaging, supported payment methods, account eligibility, compliance status, and runtime outcomes require current, merchant-specific verification.

quotes.text:
Tokenization is the process of replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive equivalent, called a token. For payments, a token represents the shopper's payment details, such as the [Primary Account Number (PAN)](/get-started-with-adyen/adyen-glossary/#card-number-pan).

If the shopper consents to save their payment details, we store payment details in the Adyen Vault. When the shopper chooses to pay with their saved payment details, you make the payment with a token. Tokens reduce your security risks and lowers your [PCI DSS](/development-resources/pci-dss-compliance-guide/) scope.

quotes.text:
* The **Sessions flow** is the simplest way to store payment details. It minimizes your [security requirements](#security-and-compliance) by creating a secure session that contains all the information needed for our client-side components to securely create and pay with tokens. This implementation qualifies you for the simplest form of PCI validation [(SAQ A)](/development-resources/pci-dss-compliance-guide/saq-a-eligibility/).

* The **Advanced flow** gives you more control over your checkout experience. You use our client-side components, or your own front-end, to collect payment details before sending them to your server to make an API call. It also requires you to manage the data flow and state yourself, offering greater flexibility for complex integrations.

The available recurring payment types depend on your server-side flow. If you use the Sessions flow, you must also use the [/payments](https://docs.adyen.com/api-explorer/Checkout/latest/post/payments) endpoint to make token payments where the shopper is not present, such as subscription payments.

When you store a shopper's payment details, you must store the token with a unique shopper reference. This shopper reference must be unique to each shopper, because we use it to associate the token with the shopper.

By default, shopper references and tokens can only be used with one [merchant account](/account/account-structure/#merchant-accounts). If your company account has multiple merchant accounts, you can enable the Token Groups feature which shares shopper references and their associated tokens between your merchant accounts. Contact our [Support Team](https://ca-test.adyen.com/ca/ca/contactUs/support.shtml?form=other) to enable the feature.

To collect raw card data, you need to be fully PCI DSS compliant. If you are fully PCI DSS compliant, you can either create your own token vault or store raw card data to offer faster checkout options.

## Definition

Adyen tokenization replaces sensitive payment details with a token. The 2026-09-15 guide calls Tokenize an Adyen Uplift module. With shopper consent, Adyen stores the details in the Adyen Vault; the merchant uses the token for later one-click, subscription, or non-fixed-schedule payments. Sessions and Advanced are distinct server-side implementation routes, and a Sessions integration still uses `/payments` for shopper-not-present token payments. [[source-adyen-docs-online-payments-tokenization]]

## Scope boundaries

A token must be associated with a shopper-unique reference. References and tokens are limited to one merchant account by default; cross-merchant-account sharing requires Support-enabled Token Groups. Collecting raw card data requires full PCI DSS compliance. The documentation snapshot does not prove current eligibility, enablement, compliance status, payment-method availability, or successful execution.
